title: Banking Collapse and Hyperinflation Devastate Economy
reason: Core facts confirm for 1996: bank runs that began in late 1995 accelerated through 1996, and roughly one-third of the banking sector (commonly cited as 14 banks) failed/entered bankruptcy proceedings in 1996 — this matches "more than a dozen banks failing simultaneously." However, two magnitude/timing details are materially off: (1) the lev's collapse from ~70.7:1 to 350:1 (Jan-Nov 1996) is an ~80% loss within calendar 1996 — the currency didn't cross the ~90%+ mark until it passed 3000:1 right at the turn of 1996/1997, so the full "90 percent" loss is really a late-1996-into-early-1997 event, not one completed within 1996; (2) "hyperinflation reached 300 percent monthly" overstates 1996 itself — year-on-year (Dec/Dec) inflation for 1996 was ~311%, but true monthly hyperinflation (Cagan-threshold, >50%/month) only began in Jan-Feb 1997, peaking at ~242% in February 1997, not 300% and not within 1996. So the description conflates the annual 1996 inflation figure with a monthly rate that actually belongs to early 1997. Country and the core banking-collapse event hold for 1996, but the hyperinflation-magnitude and full currency-collapse figures are drawn from the crisis's 1997 continuation rather than calendar 1996 itself.

title: Corporate Commercial Bank Collapse Freezes 200,000 Depositors
reason: Well-corroborated by multiple independent sources. Corporate Commercial Bank (KTB/Corpbank), confirmed as Bulgaria's fourth-largest bank by assets (end of Nov 2013), suffered a bank run in June 2014 triggered by allegations of massive fraud and related-party lending — Forbes and Bulgarian outlets detail that ~72% of its 5.2bn BGN loan portfolio (3.7bn BGN) went to shell companies controlled by owner Tsvetan Vasilev and politically connected figures (Delyan Peevski, Ahmed Dogan). The BNB placed the bank under special administration after the run and withdrew its license on 6 Nov 2014, freezing depositor access for ~6 months. On depositor count: sources give ~250,000-300,000 individuals plus ~6,000 businesses holding guaranteed deposits (up to 196,000 BGN each), with 111,981 actually claiming payouts by 2019 — the description's "200,000 depositors" is within the credible range reported (close to but slightly under the commonly cited 250,000 figure) and is materially accurate as an order-of-magnitude/scope claim. Cost to the state: guaranteed deposits totaled ~3.686-3.7 billion leva (matches description's "3.7 billion leva" almost exactly), funded via a ~2bn leva state loan to the underfunded Deposit Insurance Fund. All core facts (country=Bulgaria, year=2014, bank identity, fraud/related-party lending mechanism, deposit freeze, ~3.7bn leva resolution cost) check out via independent sources (Wikipedia, Forbes, Mediapool.bg, Capital.bg), none of which are on the off-limits list.

title: Bulgaria Joins ERM II â€” Euro Adoption Process Begins
reason: Confirmed by multiple independent sources: Bulgaria (together with Croatia) formally joined the Exchange Rate Mechanism II (ERM II) on 10 July 2020, with the lev's central rate fixed at EUR 1 = BGN 1.95583 (the pre-existing currency board rate) within a standard ±15% fluctuation band. This is the official first step of the eurozone accession process. The description's claim that persistently elevated inflation delayed actual euro adoption beyond 2024 is also consistent with reporting — Bulgaria did not adopt the euro until it exited ERM II at end of 2025 to join on 1 January 2026, well beyond the originally hoped-for 2024 target. All material details (country, year, month, mechanism, institutional significance) check out.
